source.title: Humanity's Last Code Exam: Can Advanced LLMs Conquer Human's Hardest Code Competition?
source.authors: Xiangyang Li; Xiaopeng Li; Kuicai Dong; Quanhu Zhang; Rongju Ruan; Xinyi Dai; Xiaoshuang Liu; Shengchun Xu; Yasheng Wang; Ruiming Tang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures test-time output-token scaling on code-generation pass@1, not the pretraining-loss scaling laws or other behaviors specified in the claim versions. It cites pretraining scaling laws but does not test them.
record.gate_note: Section 4.3 reports pass@1 against average output tokens during inference. This is a distinct test-time scaling result, not a result on held-out pretraining cross-entropy, parameter count, training tokens or training compute, compute-optimal allocation, architecture sensitivity, or the listed downstream-predictability version. Rows below record the related test-time result under versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: This is a code benchmark paper. Its only scaling result (Sec. 4.3) bins inference outputs by output-token count and reports ICPC pass@1. No result involves pretraining loss, parameters, training tokens or compute, allocation, architecture shape, other training regimes, or downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss. Hoffmann et al. is only cited in the Discussion as an analogy. None of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that pass@1 rises with output length for reasoning and non-reasoning models, and that test-time scaling has not reached its limit. Their headline result is that HLCE is very hard: o4-mini(high) reaches 15.85% pass@1.
record.recipe_differences: Measures inference-time output-token scaling and code-generation pass@1, rather than fitting pretraining loss against model parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper groups outputs by token count and reports the trend separately for each model; no additional controlled setting sensitivity is stated.

fits_no_version.finding: For 12 API models, ICPC World Finals pass@1 rises across bins of average output tokens (Fig. 3). The authors say this continues for o4-mini(high) and Gemini-2.5-Pro. The relation is correlational: responses are grouped post hoc by length, not given controlled budgets. Token ranges per model are narrow (e.g. about 590–640 tokens), and no power law is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time (test-time) compute scaling: longer reasoning outputs are associated with higher pass@1 on hard competitive programming problems.

record.problems: The test-time scaling curves are presented as figures without numerical point values or reported uncertainty. The paper states that only five responses were generated per question for reasoning models, citing API pricing and inference latency limits.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits extrapolated to larger runs.
No power-law fits in other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Pass@1 is related to inference output length, not to model scale or pretraining loss. Model sizes are not stated.
No exponent fitting or fit-choice comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The row states describe the study's own test-time trend, not any claim version, so versions stay ['none']. Per-model values are figure-only and could not be checked against text numbers. The token-binning design confounds length with problem difficulty, which weakens even the test-time result. Sec. 4.1 lists o1 but the results report o4-mini(high).

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or scaling against parameter count, training tokens, or training compute is measured.
No small-run fits are compared with larger-run pretraining losses.
No fixed training-compute budget or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is measured.
No architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count are reported.
No power-law comparison across other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer is reported.
The paper measures code-generation performance against inference output-token count, not downstream performance against model scale or pretraining loss.
No fit-dependence, exponent disagreement, or bending of pretraining scaling curves is examined.

relation.reason: Section 5 cites Hoffmann et al. as a pretraining-scaling analogy; its own results concern inference output length, without testing the catalogued versions.

tranche.reason: The study bins inference outputs by length and measures ICPC pass@1. It neither tests V1–V7 nor uses their power-law findings as a tool.

source_check.notes: Section 4.3 reports an association across output-length groups, without a fitted power law or controlled inference-budget intervention. Figure 3b abbreviates the reasoning Claude label and names Gemini as a preview; Table 2 supports the pack's 15.85% headline despite 15.1% elsewhere.
